title: How to fix a video editor not working on Mac during a project emergency
metaTitle: Video editor not working: emergency diagnostics for Mac editors
description: If your video editor is not working on your Mac, follow these diagnostic steps to fix crashes, export failures, and performance issues fast.
intro: When your video editor is not working, it is often because of a resource conflict or a corrupted file. You can fix most of these emergencies by checking your system logs and managing your storage before you lose any more time.
tldr: Use Activity Monitor to find memory-hogging background tasks.
Clear your cache files to stop playback stuttering.
Check your drive space to prevent export crashes.
Use proxies to improve performance on older Macs.
Restart your Mac to clear temporary system errors.

blocks.text: Why your video editor is not working

When a video editor stops working, it is usually a sign that your Mac is struggling to process the data load. This happens when your RAM is full or your storage drive is nearly at capacity. Files become fragmented and your software cannot read them fast enough to keep up with your timeline.

Another common cause is a plugin conflict. If you recently updated your macOS or your editing app, an older plugin might be causing a memory leak. This forces the app to crash whenever you try to render an effect or export your sequence.
How to diagnose a crash in Activity Monitor

Open Activity Monitor by pressing ⌘ + Space, typing Activity Monitor, and hitting Return. Click the Memory tab to see which apps are using the most RAM. If you see a process named after your editing software using more than 80% of your available memory, that is your problem.

You can also check the CPU tab to see if a background process is spiking. Sometimes a cloud sync app like Dropbox or Google Drive will try to sync your project files while you are editing. This creates a file lock that makes your video editor freeze.

If your video editor is not working because playback is stuttering, you are likely trying to edit raw 4K or 8K footage directly. Your Mac has to decode these high-resolution files in real-time, which is a heavy task.

The fix is to create proxy files. These are smaller, lower-resolution versions of your footage that are easier for your Mac to handle. In Adobe Premiere Pro, you can right-click your clips in the Project panel, select Proxy, and then Create Proxies. Once these are generated, toggle the Proxy button in your Program Monitor to start using them.
Clearing cache files to restore stability

Editing software creates temporary cache files to speed up playback. If these files get corrupted, they can cause your entire project to crash. You should clear your media cache regularly to prevent this.

In DaVinci Resolve, go to Preferences > System > Media Storage and look for your cache location. You can delete the contents of these folders to force the app to rebuild its cache. This often solves issues where the timeline is not rendering or the app is hanging during export.
Managing storage to prevent export failures
Export failures are often caused by a lack of disk space. When you export a video, your Mac needs enough room to write the final file. If your drive is full, the export will fail at the last second.

Check your available space by opening Finder and pressing ⌘ + ⇧ + C to view your drives. You should always keep at least 20% of your total drive space free for temporary files and cache. If you are low on space, move your old project files to an external SSD using a tool like Carbon Copy Cloner.

faq.question: Why does my video editor crash during export?
faq.answer: This is often due to insufficient disk space or a corrupted codec. Check your drive space, update your graphics drivers, and try exporting a small section of the timeline to isolate the problem.

faq.question: Is it safe to delete media cache files?
faq.answer: Yes, it is perfectly safe. Deleting media cache files only forces the software to re-index your project. It does not delete your original footage or your project edits.

faq.question: How do I know if my Mac is the problem?
faq.answer: Use Activity Monitor to check your system resources. If your CPU or RAM usage is hitting 100%, your Mac is struggling to keep up with the project demands.
